dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Meaningful access: AI uptake cannot close justice gaps
st.an: The source predicts broad transformation in professional and personal interactions and stresses lawyers’ responsibilities, but it does not address whether AI uptake can produce meaningful legal access or close the justice gap. Its general enthusiasm and risk awareness therefore do not establish a position on the cluster’s central proposition.
qs: I think it is going to fundamentally change how all of us interact as professionals and also in our personal lives.

I think it's important to recognize that there are risks and there are professional responsibilities, in particular for lawyers or other professionals, in how they use AI, and when they do, and how they talk to their clients about it.

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The source accepts that AI will eliminate or relocate some existing legal work and adds a concrete training response: technology-team rotations treated as part of associate development. This materially supports reconstructed apprenticeship, though it does not directly examine the verification-experience paradox or show that such rotations reproduce broader legal judgment.
qs: You know, like it's just honest and frank and clear-eyed to say this work is going away, and it's optimistic to say we're going to plan for that and try to get ahead of it.

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: The source accepts that AI will reshape delivery economics and adds a concrete firm-level model: ClearyX combines technology-enabled service delivery with integrated technologists, while proposed associate rotations address capability development and fixed-fee or subscription models respond to pricing pressure. Its claims remain qualified and largely experiential rather than independently measured.
qs: And I think, and maybe it's as much a hope as a belief, that AI is going to be a catalyst for changing the traditional billing model and focusing more on value.

st.t: In-house adoption: Stronger buyers may insource selectively
st.an: The source accepts that AI-enabled legal delivery can be shaped around corporate clients, but extends the cluster chiefly from the provider side. Cleary’s combined build-and-buy model shows how a law firm can use commercial tools, develop narrowly tailored client solutions and retain proximity-based service advantages—supporting the cluster’s non-zero-sum account of collaboration and productised expertise rather than demonstrating in-house substitution or reduced external spending.
qs: So we wanted to have the ability in-house to develop things quickly that are often more narrowly tailored.
The goal here is to harness technology to better serve our clients.

st.t: Legal consolidation: Acquisitions create integration work first
st.an: The source develops the cluster’s build-or-buy analysis by adding concrete purchasing criteria—development time, use-case durability and internal technical capacity—and by arguing that in-house technologists improve vendor assessment, customisation and product feedback. It does not provide evidence about post-acquisition integration outcomes.
qs: How long will those use cases remain viable?
I think there's a real value add to having technologists who can assess the tools, can give feedback to the product designers at those companies, can modify the tools for our own use.

st.t: Production model: Institutional absorption governs AI value
st.an: The source accepts that AI’s value depends on organisational transformation rather than access alone, and materially extends the cluster by identifying an internal technical capability that improves procurement, tool adaptation and product development. It also links adoption to client competition and potential pressure on the billable-hour model, while treating broader transformation as an early-stage forecast rather than a measured outcome.
qs: I think there's a real value add to having technologists who can assess the tools, can give feedback to the product designers at those companies, can modify the tools for our own use.

So we often hear people say the lawyers are reluctant to take up AI because it threatens the billable hour model, but look, I mean, some lawyers are going to do it, and once some lawyers do it, then everybody else has to follow because clients will get better service from the lawyers that do it, and I think he's showing us what leading the way looks like.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: The source accepts that AI will restructure routine legal production rather than eliminate lawyers, and materially extends the cluster through ClearyX as an organisational case study: a law-firm-owned technology-services business replacing traditional diligence methods, using fixed-fee delivery, and developing technical capabilities in response to client pressure. Its broader transformation claims remain forecasts rather than measured performance or ROI evidence.
qs: But the point in the conversation with partners was that work is going to go away over time and we can either be doing it ourselves through a different approach or we can watch others do it.
Those tend to be fixed fee arrangements, and we should talk at some point here about the implications of AI on traditional billing models.

st.t: Service redesign: Resistance reflects incentives and identity
st.an: The source accepts that legal AI adoption is organisational and service redesign rather than a software purchase, and materially develops that view through Cleary’s account of client design partnerships, change management, multidisciplinary technical capability and sustainable staffing economics. Its claims remain based on organisational experience and forecasts rather than measured transformation outcomes.
qs: Here's how you might think about change management within your own organization as you start to bring those tools in.
I think there's a real value add to having technologists who can assess the tools, can give feedback to the product designers at those companies, can modify the tools for our own use.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts selective, human-led deployment and materially extends the cluster with Cleary’s operating model: coordinated specialist teams, practice-level adoption, usage monitoring, controlled testing and redesigned project management. Its fixed-price ClearyX model also concretely illustrates how workflow redesign can reshape delivery and pricing, while claims that routine work will disappear remain predictive.
qs: And so the leadership of ClearyX, Springbok or AI Acceleration and DLT are talking to each other to traffic cop, like where does this make sense?
What I expect is that they are going to change the way that they are managing projects and managing teams, so that the associates and other members of the team are fully utilizing the technology.

st.t: Expertise pipeline: Automated work weakens succession routes
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s principal proposition by forecasting that routinised work will leave law firms, concentrating elite-firm work around partners and requiring proactive adaptation. It reinforces pressure on traditional staffing and development structures but offers no concrete apprenticeship, succession-funding or training model, relying mainly on qualitative forecasts.
qs: You know, like it's just honest and frank and clear-eyed to say this work is going away, and it's optimistic to say we're going to plan for that and try to get ahead of it.

st.t: Task substitution: Complementarity can still reshape staffing
st.an: The source broadly supports the proposition that AI is more than an efficiency tool and may fundamentally reshape legal practice, while retaining lawyers’ professional responsibilities. Its contribution is predictive and general, however: it does not specify task substitution, staffing changes, business-model effects or employment outcomes.
qs: I think it is going to fundamentally change how all of us interact as professionals and also in our personal lives.

I think it's important to recognize that there are risks and there are professional responsibilities, in particular for lawyers or other professionals, in how they use AI, and when they do, and how they talk to their clients about it.

kp.k: AI promises transformation beyond earlier legal technology
kp.d: Gerstenzang contrasts AI with earlier technologies that primarily accelerated existing work and increased mobility. He predicts fundamental professional and personal change, while acknowledging risks, professional responsibilities and client communication obligations. His expectation that change is likelier within two years than ten is explicitly an optimistic judgment, not a measured forecast.
qs: And so technology improved and facilitated what we were doing, but didn't fundamentally change how we were approaching client work or our own business operations.

I think it's important to recognize that there are risks and there are professional responsibilities, in particular for lawyers or other professionals, in how they use AI, and when they do, and how they talk to their clients about it.
I don't know the answer to that question, but I think it's much more likely to be two years than ten years.

kp.k: ClearyX originated in client pressure over diligence costs
kp.d: Gerstenzang says the firm began considering greater technology use in 2021, identifying transactional diligence as a client pain point. ClearyX began as a technology services subsidiary focused on diligence and subsequently expanded into virtual data rooms, contract lifecycle management and other services. He credits this pre-generative-AI initiative with fostering partners' adaptability toward subsequent AI adoption.
qs: So we in 2021 started thinking about how to bring technology more into our practice.
clients were kind of tired of paying big law rates for work that could be done more effectively and more efficiently.
the real difference maker of ClearyX was that it created a mindset among our partners of adaptability and openness to bring technology into what we do.

kp.k: Subsidiary autonomy supports differentiated services and nonlawyer incentives
kp.d: Gerstenzang describes ClearyX as wholly owned but substantially autonomous, preserving a startup culture rather than replicating a law firm. It serves Cleary matters, clients' in-house projects and projects involving competing firms. Cleary applies firm conflicts and client checks, but Gerstenzang says ClearyX does not practise law, permitting more flexible nonlawyer compensation. Its tracking equity is not described as current outside ownership.
qs: And so it is wholly owned by the firm, but operates with a significant degree of autonomy.
we do treat ClearyX as part of the firm for conflicts purposes
But they're not engaged in the practice of law, and that gives us more flexibility, for example, to bring in senior non-lawyer professionals into ClearyX
Well, it's today wholly owned, but there's a kind of a tracking equity that over time the senior professionals will realize on.

kp.k: Internal comparisons supported cheaper technology-enabled diligence
kp.d: Gerstenzang reports that early ClearyX diligence was compared with traditional diligence on the same M&A deals to address partner concerns about quality and reputation. He says quality was on par or better and costs roughly half those of traditional diligence. These are reported internal findings: the transcript supplies no sample size, scoring protocol or detailed results, and the comparisons concerned the earlier technology initiative rather than a specified generative-AI evaluation.
qs: And we did a series of AB studies where the diligence was done both by ClearyX and in the traditional way on the same deal.
And pretty quickly we saw that the ClearyX quality was on par or better.
And the cost is roughly half for ClearyX due diligence versus a traditional due diligence exercise.

kp.k: Diligence automation responds to work already leaving BigLaw
kp.d: Gerstenzang says partners worried about replacing associate hours, but clients were already assigning diligence to cheaper national firms while retaining Cleary for the main transaction. His argument is that preserving traditional high-margin diligence is not a sustainable alternative: the firm should retain participation through a different delivery model. He predicts declining traditional diligence work without quantifying lawyer displacement.
qs: The second concern that people raise, well, what are we gonna, like what happens to all those hours?
we're gonna hire this other firm, very good national firm to do the diligence and they're much cheaper than you.
that work is going to go away over time and we can either be doing it ourselves through a different approach or we can watch others do it.

kp.k: Incremental investment limits the partnership's long-term funding problem
kp.d: Gerstenzang acknowledges partnership investment constraints but reports broad support at Cleary and an incremental approach rather than large speculative upfront expenditure. He says ClearyX was profitable almost from inception and had about 40 people. In their debrief, the hosts argue that relatively quick returns and gradual costs qualify, rather than disprove, structural investment concerns; their suggestion that Springbok's purchase price largely takes the form of future salaries is speculation, not disclosed transaction evidence.
qs: not to just make some big upfront investment, hope it works, but to grow both ClearyX and now Springbok in an incremental way.
And ClearyX has become a profitable business almost from the beginning.
And today, it's about 40 people
which suggests to me that most of the purchase price probably will be paid over time in the form of salary to the employees.

kp.k: Springbok acquisition internalised technology, talent and development capacity
kp.d: Gerstenzang says Springbok previously developed and consulted on technology for law firms and in-house departments, including Cleary. Following discussions lasting more than a year, Cleary acquired its people and technology 'earlier this year' and ended its external business. The acquired team formed the core of the broader AI Acceleration Team, distinct from ClearyX; approximately a dozen initial people had doubled by the interview, against about 1,300 lawyers globally.
qs: And then earlier this year, we bought Springbok AI and all of the people came over to join Cleary Gottlieb.
We weren't interested in kind of operating Springbok as a kind of going concern, but really bringing it fully in house and now deploying it to our people and to our clients.
The AI acceleration team is not just comprised of the former Springbok people, it's a broader team.
That was about a dozen people, and we're double that now.

kp.k: Technologists must become partners in client service
kp.d: Gerstenzang argues that law firms struggle to recruit and retain senior technologists when they lack influence and recognition relative to lawyers. An established technical team supplies recruiting credibility and expertise to assess further hires. He reports joint lawyer-technologist pitches and project execution, and recommends treating technology professionals as client-service collaborators rather than merely infrastructure support.
qs: Because they don't feel like they have a seat at the table the way that the senior lawyers do.
It's much easier to go from 15 to 50 data scientists than it is to go from 0 to 2 or 2 to 5.
we need our lawyers at every level to embrace technologists as partners in client service.
we are pitching together our lawyers and our technologists for big projects. And we are executing those projects together.

kp.k: Buying remains default; internal development fills specific gaps
kp.d: Gerstenzang rejects a strict make-versus-buy choice: Cleary licenses and evaluates products including Harvey, Legora and Deep Judge, while developing bespoke solutions where available products or vendor timelines do not meet needs. Internal development decisions consider time, use cases and their likely duration. He explicitly disclaims building a foundational model or competing as a general technology company.
qs: our approach has been to do both, to both make and to buy.
including Harvey and Legora and Deep Judge.
our default is to buy it, not to make it.
What we are making is where there's a gap.
we are not trying to build our own LLM.

kp.k: Bespoke tools automate billing administration and customise vendor products
kp.d: Gerstenzang illustrates internal development with a tool categorising a year's billing diaries into 50 client-defined buckets, previously work for paralegals, associates and partners. He reports an initial working solution and anticipates a desktop version within weeks. More generally, the team modifies off-the-shelf tools to meet narrow client or matter requirements that remain unresolved by standard products.
qs: wants the year's worth of diaries bucketed in 50 different buckets.
before Springbok AI, that would have been the job of paralegals and associates and partners
Springbok designed for us a tool that with relatively straightforward prompts can go through a year's worth of diaries and put it into the 50 buckets.
The off-the-shelf tool gets you almost there, but not quite for what the particular client or project calls for.

kp.k: Coordinated teams and usage analytics guide AI deployment
kp.d: Gerstenzang describes coordination among ClearyX, AI Acceleration and Discovery Litigation Technology, the latter launched almost 20 years earlier. Their leaders route requests and share developments rather than requiring lawyers or clients to navigate organisational boundaries. Practice-group advocates identify uses, while Legora analytics track adoption by functionality, seniority and practice. He reports approximately 1200 active Legora users; this is adoption evidence, not a productivity or quality measure.
qs: DLT, Discovery Litigation Technology.
that's a business, actually, that we launched almost 20 years ago
we're not asking all of our lawyers and certainly not our clients to figure out what part of our technology team they should be talking to.
we have like 1200 active users of Legora across the firm.
What your people are doing, that's critically important.

kp.k: Partners should enable adoption rather than master every tool
kp.d: Gerstenzang describes partnership governance through transparent discussion rather than threatened sanctions. He expects partners to gain sufficient confidence to change project and team management, insist on appropriate team AI use, and support associates and technologists. Clients' requests for technology-enabled work and assistance with their own legal departments' technology journeys helped secure partner support.
qs: I don't expect our partners to all become masters of the use of AI.
What I expect is that they are going to change the way that they are managing projects and managing teams, so that the associates and other members of the team are fully utilizing the technology.
Don't build the wall and support the building of the windmills.
how we could help them on their own technology journey within legal departments.

kp.k: Fixed-fee diligence separates technology services from legal advice
kp.d: Gerstenzang explains that ClearyX agrees a fixed price based on document and page counts, document characteristics and outputs, including summaries, analysis and a portal. Cleary Gottlieb's legal advice is billed separately. He presents the portal's usability, customisability and continuing post-closing integration utility as important client-value differentiators, not merely its underlying technology.
qs: Those tend to be fixed fee arrangements
So if there is legal advice because Cleary Gottlieb lawyers are involved, that's charged separately in one way or another.

the diligence component of it, the summarization of documents, the analysis, the creation of a portal that allows the client to look either at summaries or at underlying documents or whatever, that's all done at a fixed price.
So that if you want to use that as a kind of post-acquisition integration tool, you can do that too.

kp.k: AI may catalyse value-based and recurring pricing
kp.d: Gerstenzang criticises hourly billing for clients' perceived inefficiency incentives and firms' inability to capture creativity, judgment and differentiated insights. He hopes AI will accelerate fixed-fee, subscription and value-oriented arrangements, increasing predictability while making firms responsible for resource efficiency. Licensing proprietary tools and ongoing technology connectivity are envisaged alongside matter work. Billing for compute, engineers and related consulting remains under discussion, rather than an established firm-wide model.
qs: the billable hour approach does not reward creativity or judgment or differentiated insights.
maybe it's as much a hope as a belief, that AI is going to be a catalyst for changing the traditional billing model and focusing more on value.
And then it's up to us to manage our resources in the most efficient way.
a kind of subscription model is the more sensible economic model for that kind of service.
Well, we're talking about all those things.

kp.k: Outside capital is considered for growth, not partner distributions
kp.d: Gerstenzang reports inbound interest in significant minority investment in ClearyX, but says the firm is not interested in selling it. He identifies affiliation, brand, quality control and access to Cleary's substantive expertise as important value sources. Any third-party capital would need a clear growth strategy; hosts subsequently speculate about windfalls and retention incentives, without reporting an actual investment or distribution.
qs: We're not interested in selling ClearyX.
we have had inbound interest in significant minority investment in ClearyX.
And that today is not about distributing it up to the firm and to our partners.
It's about what's the growth strategy that we can power with that third party capital.

kp.k: Client co-design differentiates the firm's technology offering
kp.d: Responding to possible competition from better-funded technology providers, Gerstenzang argues that client proximity and narrowly tailored solutions are Cleary's advantages. He describes design partnerships combining client and firm lawyers with technologists to develop workflows and technology. Related assistance extends beyond legal advice to tool selection, change management and coordination with clients' other law firms; he qualifies bespoke delivery as neither universally best nor the only approach.
qs: We're trying to solve problems for specific clients in specific projects.
we have actually a kind of collaboration and a design partnership with the client for a particular thing that they're trying to do.
I'm not saying that that will always be the best approach. It will certainly not be the only approach.
the service we're providing is not legal advice. It's more in the nature of consulting advice.

kp.k: Technical capability supports purchasing judgment and rapid experimentation
kp.d: Gerstenzang says in-house technologists improve tool assessment, vendor feedback, modification and product-development decisions. Given rapidly shifting model capabilities, he recommends remaining as LLM-agnostic as possible, experimenting, abandoning unsuitable tools quickly and revisiting them after three or six months. This approach deliberately resists institutional pressure to lock into one platform after training everyone.
qs: technologists who can assess the tools, can give feedback to the product designers at those companies, can modify the tools for our own use.
you need to do as much as you can in an LLM agnostic way.
let's try lots of things and be willing to say, you know what, that's not what we need for now and come back to it in three months or six months because maybe it's changed.

kp.k: Technology rotations could become part of associate formation
kp.d: Gerstenzang anticipates recruiting lawyers with technology skills and an adaptable mindset, some of whom will code. He describes an early-stage proposal, not an implemented programme, allowing interested associates to spend six months or a year in AI Acceleration as a recognised training rotation alongside traditional practice placements.
qs: They will be technology savvy. They're certainly going to have a technology and adaptability mindset.

maybe we should have a kind of rotation opportunity so that lawyers who have an interest in technology can spend part of their associate career, it could be six months or a year, within the AI Acceleration Team and treat that as part of their training

kp.k: AI could alter scale advantages and enable transactional boutiques
kp.d: Gerstenzang argues that AI requires reconsidering consolidation and firm scale, while stressing that implications remain uncertain. Using earlier litigation technologies as an analogy, he says online research and e-discovery reduced the need for expensive libraries and large document-review teams, somewhat levelling competition for boutiques. He suggests analogous transactional boutiques may emerge; this is a prediction rather than evidence of an observed AI-driven market shift.
qs: this question of scale and consolidation has to be reevaluated through the lens of AI.
technology kind of leveled the playing field somewhat for boutique litigation firms versus Biglaw.
I think we shouldn't be surprised at the development of boutique transactional practices that are akin to the boutique litigation practices that that are successful today.
I think that's an open question.

kp.k: Hosts foresee routinised work migrating outside law firms
kp.d: In the post-interview discussion, the hosts envisage sophisticated partners retaining high-value work while increasing reliance on AI or external businesses for other tasks. John specifically predicts that work performed almost entirely by AI is unlikely to remain inside law firms and may move to clients or third-party providers. These are hosts' market hypotheses, not Gerstenzang's reported findings; the discussion includes software-as-a-service provision as well as work delivery.
qs: if there's an element of legal work that really can be done almost entirely with AI, it probably won't be done inside of a law firm at all.
if something is so routinized that you can do the great bulk of it with software, then it really just shouldn't be done in a law firm.
Yeah. Or with a third-party service provider.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Michael Gerstenzang predicts fundamental changes to legal work, pricing, professional roles and competition, while describing Cleary’s current technology-enabled services and internal AI development.
pts.d: Gerstenzang distinguishes AI from earlier technologies that primarily accelerated existing practices: he expects AI to change professional interactions fundamentally. He argues that conventional high-priced due diligence will migrate to cheaper delivery models, making adaptation a way to retain work rather than simply cannibalize associate hours. He reports that ClearyX delivers technology-enabled diligence at roughly half the traditional cost with comparable or better quality; this experience began before the current generative-AI wave and is not presented as an isolated measure of generative-AI performance. Cleary’s AI strategy combines purchased products with bespoke development and customization, rather than building foundational models or competing as a general-purpose technology company. An example is a Springbok-developed tool that categorizes a year’s billing diaries into client-required buckets. He expects technologists to become partners in client service, partners to manage AI-using teams, and future lawyers increasingly to possess technological skills, potentially including coding. He suggests AI could catalyze movement away from hourly billing toward value, fixed fees and subscriptions, explicitly describing this partly as a hope. He envisages ongoing technology relationships and consulting support for clients’ own adoption, beyond individual legal transactions. Finally, he suggests AI could enable transactional boutiques comparable to successful litigation boutiques, leaving the implications for consolidation unresolved.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence is principally Gerstenzang’s account of Cleary’s operations, internal comparisons and client experience; broader market forecasts are arguments and analogies rather than measured forecasts.
pts.d: At 00:38:12–00:39:27, Gerstenzang describes internal AB comparisons of ClearyX and traditional diligence on the same M&A deals, reporting quality on par or better and costs roughly half as large. No sample size, scoring methodology, numerical quality results or independent validation is supplied. He also recounts clients moving diligence to cheaper national firms before ClearyX launched. Operational examples include billing-diary categorization, tailoring off-the-shelf tools, joint lawyer–technologist pitches and projects, fixed-price diligence with separately charged legal advice, and client use of a portal after closing. He reports ClearyX was profitable almost from inception and had about 40 people, while the acquired Springbok team grew from approximately 12 to twice that size within the broader AI acceleration team. He reports approximately 1,200 active Legora users and tracking of usage by functionality and seniority; these establish reported adoption, not measured productivity gains. His talent argument draws on acquisition and recruitment experience: an established technical team supplies credibility and expertise for further hiring and product evaluation. His boutique forecast relies on an analogy with earlier legal research and e-discovery technologies lowering litigation infrastructure requirements. The source offers no market-wide causal study establishing AI’s effects on employment, billing or consolidation.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Gerstenzang favors a relatively near-term transformation but gives no firm deadline; successful adoption depends on professional responsibility, organizational integration and selective, adaptable investment.
pts.d: Speaking in the episode labeled 2026, Gerstenzang considers substantial change more likely within two years than ten, while explicitly saying he does not know the answer and that even five years feels long given recent progress. His historical starting point for ClearyX is technology planning in 2021, before the current generative-AI wave. The Springbok acquisition is described as occurring 'earlier this year'; the billing-diary desktop solution is expected in a matter of weeks. Proposed associate rotations of six months or a year remain an early-stage training idea, not an implemented program. He frames fully integrating non-lawyer talent as important over the next decades. Bespoke development is conditional on a gap in available products, its cost and development time, and the likely duration of the use case. He advocates remaining LLM-agnostic, experimenting and revisiting unsuitable products after three or six months rather than locking into a platform. His billing prediction remains explicitly qualified as partly hope; the bespoke approach is not claimed to be universally best, and transactional boutique growth and consolidation effects remain tentative. He also emphasizes risks and lawyers’ professional responsibilities concerning use and client communication.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claims primarily concern large commercial firms, transactional clients, in-house legal departments, lawyers and technologists, with possible competitive opportunities for boutiques.
pts.d: For corporate clients, Gerstenzang describes lower-cost diligence, predictable fixed pricing, usable document portals and continuing access after acquisitions. ClearyX does not provide legal advice; its fixed-price services are distinct from separately billed Cleary Gottlieb legal advice, and it can support matters handled by other firms or internally by clients. In-house departments are also recipients of technology and change-management consulting. For associates, paralegals and partners, tasks such as billing-diary categorization can shift to software, while traditional associate diligence hours face pressure from alternative delivery. He does not quantify resulting job losses or specify a new staffing shape. Partners need enough familiarity with AI to direct its use by their teams, rather than necessarily becoming expert users themselves. Future associates are expected to be technology-savvy, with possible rotations into the AI acceleration team. Technologists and data scientists are to gain substantive roles in client delivery rather than remain confined to infrastructure support, conditional on being genuinely integrated and valued. Large firms face competition for technical talent and pressure to change delivery and pricing; transactional boutiques may gain opportunities as technology reduces some advantages of scale. The discussion does not advance claims about access to justice or unmet individual civil legal need.
